title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

reading.body:
An attorney submitted fabricated legal citations to a court, claiming to represent a food store owner in a civil suit. The citations were generated by an AI tool and were not verified before filing. This is a failure of human oversight at the point of deployment: the attorney used an AI system to generate case law without checking whether the citations actually existed.

The fabricated cases appeared alongside a false quotation from a real case and additional citation errors in the filing submitted to Hennepin County Court. A judge discovered the problem, ruled against the attorney's client, and suspended him for 30 days. What would have caught this: basic verification that each cited case exists and matches its description, a step that either the attorney or a supervising attorney should have performed before submission.

It is not established whether the attorney understood the AI tool was prone to generating false citations, or whether he was aware of the risks before using it.

reports.title: Minnesota lawyer suspended over fake AI case citations

summary:
Minnesota attorney Faisal S. Ahmed was suspended for 30 days after submitting fake legal case citations to a court. Ahmed, who has been licensed since 2014, represented a food store owner in a civil suit and included two nonexistent cases, Anderson v. City of Biwabik and Doherty v. Alma E. Clark Memorial Home, in his legal memorandum to Hennepin County Court. The opposing attorney discovered the fabricated citations were generated by an AI tool. Ahmed also included a false quotation from a real case and two citation errors in his filing.

Judge Lois Conroy ruled against Ahmed's client and ordered the defendants to pay $233,563 in back rent. She fined Ahmed $5,000 and referred him to the Minnesota Lawyer's Professional Responsibility Board for disciplinary action. Ahmed agreed to the 30-day suspension and must pay an additional $900 in costs. This case reflects a growing problem with attorneys using AI tools without proper verification, with over 800 documented instances of fake citations already catalogued online. The court emphasized that AI should not replace proper legal analysis and interpretation.
